utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters; good morning, legal assistants, the registrar, the Office of the Prosecutor, Defence counsel. Good morning, General Krstic. We are going to continue your testimony, and, of course, you are still testifying under oath, and it is Mr. McCloskey who will take the floor now. You have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning; good morning, Your Honours, counsel, General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, first of all, I wish you to -- do you have that pointer still?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could get the General the pointer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could step to the map, which is Exhibit 2. Could you, first of all, show us on the map the Cyrillic symbols that stand for "Drina Corps" on that map?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Drina Corps" here is marked in Cyrillic letters "DK".

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you show us where the "Eastern Bosnia Corps" is marked on that map, the Cyrillic symbols?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "Eastern Bosnian Corps" is over here, again, marked in Cyrillic letters "IBK".

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can you show us where the boundary is between the Drina Corps and the Eastern Bosnia Corps? I can tell you there is a light red line that appears to have been drawn on the map just above the town of Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be this border here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we zero in on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General. Could you show us again, while we're getting a close-up, and just go on that little red line and wherever you say the border is now that we have a close-up.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this map, it is drawn here. This is the line indicated on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And could you point out where Branjevo, the village of Branjevo, is, if you know, near Pilica. You can just give us the general area, General, if you don't see where it's written.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't see it written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be somewhere here, I think, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You can go ahead and have a seat. Now, the 3.500 to 4.000 victims that you noted reading about in the UN report, do you have any reason to believe that those numbers are not accurate regarding the people that were murdered by the VRS after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that that number is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You contest it?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not contesting it, but I cannot assert that that is the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You saw the exhumation evidence. Are you contesting that the bodies that were found in the graves are victims of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not contesting the graves. As I have already said, I learnt for the first time about those gravesites in the course of this trial when the Prosecution produced evidence before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you believe or do you have any evidence to believe that any of those victims recovered from those exhumations were battle casualties?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I personally have no evidence on the basis of my previous knowledge, but what has been presented here in court is evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any indication that the people that were found in those graves were battle casualties?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The indications can be found solely on the basis of the evidence presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you do not contest the exhumation evidence in any way?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not contesting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, did you know that the Branjevo Military Farm was an asset of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I had no knowledge that the Zvornik Brigade had a farm in Branjevo. It was not at all within the framework of my activities or responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, could security officers, under your theory of the case, such as Ljubo Beara and Vujadin Popovic, take over the Kula school near Pilica, the Pilica Cultural Centre, the school -- the new school at Petkovci, the school in Orahovac and place hundreds and hundreds of prisoners in each of those schools without informing the command structure of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if they did inform the command structure of the Zvornik Brigade, what would the duty of the Zvornik Brigade be in terms of informing their superior command?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their duty was to inform or notify the superior command about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who would that have been?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the same question for taking over the Branjevo Farm. The fields near Kozluk, right next to the Drina Wolf barracks, the plateau of the dam near Petkovci, and the field just up the road from the school at Orahovac, could Ljubija Beara and Vujadin Popovic have taken and used those fields, those areas, for the murder of thousands of Bosnian Muslim men without informing the Zvornik Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. It is possible, in view of the way in which they worked and behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is possible?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is possible, General?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that they did not inform the command of the Zvornik Brigade about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, there's a war going on and this is right near the front lines; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at the same time there are large-scale combat operations going on from the direction of Tuzla, with the 2nd Corps of the BH army. Then the Zvornik Brigade is also fighting against the 28th Division. So the main concern of the brigade command at the time were the combat operations. And I don't know to what extent they had time and the means to keep watch as to what was happening deep within their area of responsibility, especially if this is being done by a superior command to them, and I mean the Main Staff, headed by Ljubo Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, automatic weapon fire is rather loud, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there was such fire all over the place in that area, starting from the area linked to the 1st Birac Brigade, up to the borderline with the Eastern Bosnian Corps, because an offensive had been relaunched at the time from Tuzla towards the positions of the Zvornik and Birac Brigades; and there were also activities by the 28th Division, then the combat activities of the Zvornik Brigade to crush that offensive, and it was hard to tell where the fire was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you heard Mr. Butler testify that on July 14th the column had not reached the area of Orahovac, there had been no major assault from the 2nd Corps, yet all day long on the 14th, from the afternoon all the way through the evening, there was sounds of automatic rifle fire in the village of Orahovac, not to mention the bulldozers and the screams of the people that were murdered. This is a few kilometres from the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade and inhabited villages right nearby. Are you truly suggesting that the Zvornik Brigade command would not have had knowledge of such an event on July 14th, and such a situation? The same holds true for Petkovci Dam. All night long. It's not on the front lines. There was no assault going on at that point at Petkovci area. The same goes for Branjevo Farm and the little town of Pilica, right in the downtown area. Are you saying that there's no way that the Zvornik Brigade would have had knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether there was fire on the front line at the time or not, only the command of the Zvornik Brigade and the battalions under its command know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's assume for Branjevo Farm, for example, that it's a military farm, military officers run it, and that in order to use that farm as an execution field, the military thing would have been done; it would have been approved through the Zvornik Brigade command. Wouldn't that be the normal way things would have worked?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowing who was in charge of this, it did not have to be approved by the command of the Zvornik Brigade at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Beara and others could have just stolen the Branjevo Farm for their own purposes and the Zvornik Brigade wouldn't have done a thing or cared or known; is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way, that they would steal it, but Ljubo Beara was the head of the security of the Main Staff, and he had the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authority to use that facility for his own purposes. It was not the first case for facilities to be usurped in that way by subordinate commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't want to get into 1992 --

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no way -- there was no way for the command of the Zvornik Brigade to resist Ljubo Beara, to oppose him, with respect to his use of that facility and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course there isn't. Orders from General Mladic. It was their duty to follow orders from General Mladic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me about Ljubo Beara?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the duty of Zvornik Brigade to follow orders of General Mladic as it comes from the Main Staff through the Drina Corps or through Ljubo Beara; it's their duty to follow orders, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe that General Mladic issued any kind of task to the Zvornik Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That wasn't my question --

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in connection with everything that was happening in the facilities in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was --

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me try again. You said the Zvornik Brigade could not resist the orders of Ljubo Beara, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So they would follow the orders of Ljubo Beara.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that Ljubo Beara did not consult them at all, because if he had consulted them, then Colonel Pandurevic would not be asking who had brought the soldiers to his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ljubo Beara is a Main Staff security officer. He's not a commander, is he?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he runs the Security Service, which has considerable authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Vujadin Popovic, as the Assistant Commander for Security, is not a commander of troops, is he?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is not, but he is in charge of the deployment of units of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He has the power to advise the commander on how those units are deployed, but he does not have the power to deploy those units outside the authority of his commander, does he?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please be able to answer these questions in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Krstic, why can't you answer this question in public? This is a very general question, simply to learn whether a security officer can have command over troops. That was the question that the Prosecutor has asked you. It's a question that has to do with the rules and regulations. I don't see why you can't answer that question. Mr. Prosecutor, will you please put your question so that I can check whether I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I can -- I think it would be best, Your Honour, if I -- it was a question regarding the structure and the power of the Assistant Commander for Security for the Drina Corps, whether or not he had the power to command troops or whether or not he had the power merely to advise troops. This is a question regarding the structure. It has not asked for personalities, family members, or any other sensitive subject that I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you see. So I have understood correctly. You can answer that question easily.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, but Mr. McCloskey -- I do apologise, but he has been mentioning names. I agree that I can answer the question if it has to do with the duties of a particular officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, answer the question without mentioning the name if that is helpful to you. Just answer the question without giving any names. Mr. McCloskey, please repeat your question so as to remind General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, in the corps command -- there is an Assistant Commander for Security in any corps command. That security person does not command troops, does he? He merely advises the commander on the appropriate use of military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. However, we have already discussed this. If that person, by order of a superior commander, is placed under somebody else's command and the entire structure of the units you are referring to is placed under the command of that officer to whom this one is subordinate, then they are in control and deploy those units in the way they see fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand what your theory of your case is, General Krstic, but again, security officers do not command troops normally, do they?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under normal conditions, they do not command troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Troops, infantry officers, commanders, brigade commanders, for instance, they're pretty tough guys. They're used to taking orders and giving orders, but they're not used to taking orders from security guys, are they?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when Vujadin Popovic comes into the Zvornik Brigade area, or Ljubo Beara comes into the Zvornik Brigade area, their only authority is the authority by which they have gained from their commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to Ljubo Beara and Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubo Beara did receive orders from his commander, but Vujadin Popovic certainly didn't receive orders from his commander, but he received them from Ljubo Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the normal course of events, if security officers come to infantry troops, infantry commanders into their area, and provide orders or information, their only authority is that gained from their commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they came among officers who were in command of units on the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Vinko Pandurevic would not follow the order of a security officer unless he felt that it was the order of the security officer's commander, would he?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to prisoners of war, he would not follow them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But somebody arranged for all these schools and all these sites and all this engineering equipment and the drivers from the 6th Battalion and the 4th Battalion infantry from the Zvornik Brigade and the MPs from the Zvornik Brigade. Somebody did that, didn't they? Somebody assisted the security people in all that, or did they do it all themselves, these two guys?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at all who helped them, that they took vehicles from the 4th Battalion to use them for whatever they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to another area. I would like to play the video of General Mladic and General Krstic and others going through the town of Srebrenica on July 11th. It should be Exhibit number 145. But before we play it, let me ask the General one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, do you have a nickname or a shortened name that some officers refer to you as?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have a nickname of any kind; I just have an abbreviation of my surname. And with that shortened -- abbreviation of my surname, my subordinates never referred to me by that name; they always addressed me as is prescribed by the rules and regulations when it comes to relationships between superior officers and subordinates in the army. So I said my subordinates never used that abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember when Mr. Ruez asked you that same question and you said you didn't have a nickname and you -- and such things weren't used?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a nickname. As I said, it's an abbreviation of my last name. A nickname is something else again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see. So you didn't tell Mr. Ruez about the abbreviation of your last name; you just were talking about you didn't have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were being completely honest with Mr. Ruez on that point?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was being completely honest, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, General Mladic refers to you by this shortened name, does he not?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's his right. I had no right to be angry with him for doing so, for calling me in the way he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On July 11th, as you were beginning to walk into Srebrenica, did you have any reason to be angry with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was all very strange to me, what happened with respect to the entrance to Srebrenica, and I spoke about that during my testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, lots of things have been very strange, but my question was: Did you have any reason to be angry with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have been angry in myself with Mr. Mladic, but it was his right to decide whether he was going to enter Srebrenica or not -- it was not up to me -- and, of course, his overall behaviour in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was not whether you could have been mad, General, but my question was whether or not you were angry or mad at General Mladic on July 11th, during the time that you walked through town.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find the question strange. I really do apologise. I have already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, were you or were you not angry with General Mladic on July 11th as you walked through the town?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In myself, I was mad, yes, within me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could play 145/1, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, General Krstic, what is your shortened name?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The name we saw General Mladic refer to you as.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he said first "Krstic." He referred to me by the name "Krstic" first and then said "Krle."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the same "Krle" we've seen in the intercepts? Or the same word, I should say.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to speak about intercepts. I am talking in concrete terms about this situation and in relation to the concrete situation that we saw a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The word Krle, K-r-l-e, was seen in transcripts of Bosnian intercepts; is that correct? The Prosecution's evidence, whether you believe it is valid or not, it was seen as part of this case?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, before coming into town, we've seen a video of the APC and you and General Mladic, and we didn't play that, but I would like Exhibit 157 put on the ELMO for a moment, if we could. Can you take the pointer and identify each of the people in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is the one in the forefront of the photograph, for the record, in the centre. Sorry, General, you need to point on the ELMO. You need to point on the ELMO so we can see your pointer. Try to speak into the microphone as best you can also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you can help him pull that microphone towards him.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this photograph, you can see the following persons: General Mladic, myself, Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, Vinko Pandurevic is to the -- immediately to the right of General Mladic, and General Krstic is immediately to the left of General Mladic. And how about the other two soldiers? Who are they?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These soldiers were from the security of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what were their names?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have your own security? You're a General.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At any time between July 5th and July 12th, did you have any security person for your personal security?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was just the security for the forward command post, not my own personal security. From the forward command post, I very rarely went anywhere. First of all, for health reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to make sure the record is clear, the nature of the record's clear, when we talk about personal security, we're not talking about the security branch in any way with this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who --

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the driver, I didn't have anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was your driver?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My driver was Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's his --

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlado. And then soldier Bjelanovic, Private Bjelanovic, another driver, and Krstic, who had the same surname as myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was that Krstic's first name?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Dalibor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any relation to you?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was a refugee from Sarajevo. No kin of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was his position relating to you?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a private soldier and a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was your driver on this trip into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was precisely that driver, Dalibor Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the other driver's name, I'm sorry, again, was Josic or Tosic?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vlado Tosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was he at the time that you were coming into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the vehicle with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did Vlado Tosic spend the night during this operation from July 5th through to July 13th?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 5th to the 13th of July, he was where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And precisely can you tell us where you spent the night during that time period?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 5th to the 11th of July, I think I spent most of my nights at the forward command post, but I spent one night in the command of the Bratunac Brigade. That was on the night between the 11th and 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did Mladic spend the night when he was at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he slept. I don't know. But he didn't spend a single night at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Dalibor Krstic also spend the night at the same place you did during this time period?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to one more brief photo exhibit, number 768. And if the monitor could be zeroed in on the face of General Krstic, which is in the right-hand side of the picture. Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you don't look angry.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you think. If you can't see that I am angry -- it is not in my nature to demonstrate my anger and feelings before my superiors --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This was a --

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or my subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This was a great moment in the history of the war for the VRS army, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. McCloskey, it is a good moment to break. Let us now take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, before resuming, I should like to make an observation in connection with your cross-examination. The Chamber has noted something. We did not interrupt so as not to break your continuity, but I would like you to pay attention, because you used -- when you mentioned the interview of General Krstic with Ruez, you used the word "honest" and "dishonest." I don't think it is up to you to judge the witness. Another observation: I think you must abstain from making comments; for example, "There were many strange things." I'm just giving you an example. It's not up to you to make comments of that kind. A third point I should like to underline: You asked General Krstic that he doesn't seem to be angry. In my opinion, that is not the right way to put the question. You could perhaps ask: "What was your mood at the time?" for instance. I could give you another example. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. General Krstic is not here to contest or demit anything. You can ask him, "What is your opinion?" You are fully entitled to do that. Or "Do you have any other information?" But don't ask him whether you contest or do not contest this or that. I have always said here that all questions must be put under one condition, that is, that they should be relevant and pertinent, and that also depends on the manner in which the question is put. I have always insisted that the question should be clear, concrete, and concise. This is something that I have always insisted upon -- clear, concrete, and concise -- because these are questions that lead to information. Whenever there is a commentary or a judgement, that is not a good way to get information. You may get a reaction from the Defence. The witness may defend himself if he feels to be harassed. So those are the remarks I wish to convey to you, and please bear this in mind. After this, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Understood. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, this photograph that is on the ELMO, can you tell us who the person is that's between General Mladic and yourself?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person between me and General Mladic is the president of the assembly of the municipality of Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Tupajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is he a military man in this capacity? Is he in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tupajic was president of the municipal assembly of Sokolac at the time, and while I was commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, he very, very frequently visited the brigade on his own or as a member of a group, and he probably did that on this occasion as well. I don't know when he came to see Colonel Trivic; whether at the beginning, when a part of the brigade was engaged there, or later on, I don't know that, but he came with him to Srebrenica. So he is not a military person. But people frequently donned uniforms in those days, especially when they went to tour units, either on their own or as part of a team. Everyone put on uniforms except clergymen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to Exhibit 158.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Three men, identified as 1, 2, and 3 in this photograph, who are clearly identified by Drazen Erdemovic as members of the 10th Diversionary Unit, and you were standing right next to them. Was the 10th Diversionary Unit with you in Srebrenica in the town in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not standing next to them; I'm just passing by them. The 10th Diversionary Detachment, throughout the duration of the operation until the entry into Srebrenica, was not at all engaged in any way. They are not mentioned in the Corps Commander's order, not even as a reserve force of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question is: Are these three men 10th Diversionary?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I simply did not observe nor did I seek to identify which unit which soldier or group of soldiers belonged to. The fact that I passed by them -- I passed by the other soldiers who were there too -- and I didn't notice anything in particular with respect to individuals or groups nor did I make an effort to learn in any way which unit they belonged to. I didn't pay attention to their uniforms, insignias on their sleeves, or anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've mentioned the -- who is the Commander of the 10th Diversionary Unit at this time?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from before that the Commander of the 10th Diversionary Detachment was Miso Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recognise Miso Pelemis? Do you know what he looks like?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him once at a celebration of the day of the Birac Brigade on the 20th of May as the Brigade Commander, because Colonel Andric invited me to this celebration as his colleague. The next day was the celebration of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, the 21st of May. That is the day when the unit was formed that was being celebrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before or after the walk through Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before. Before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you recognise Miso Pelemis in your walk through Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He is identified as on the film, and Mr. Ruez, in his direct testimony, clearly on that film. Did you see him on that film?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that photograph, but it was shown here. Mr. Erdemovic, in his testimony, spoke about his presence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall, in your earlier testimony, saying that General Mladic made an order on the 11th for the soldiers to light haystacks on fire?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't get the translation of that. Yes. Yes. Before the airstrikes and during the airstrikes and after that, General Mladic ordered that, for protection purposes, haystacks should be set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that order went out to the brigades and various units involved in the operation on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was ordered by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So would it have been communicated to the units in the field that would have been near the haystacks?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic ordered this to the brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the units in the field would have received --

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which means, yes, it was conveyed to the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall during the testimony of Drazen Erdemovic that he received an order from Miso Pelemis to light haystacks on fire?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to Exhibit number 770.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a freeze-frame of General Mladic sitting down and you're standing over him. Are you communicating with General Mladic in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Zivanovic was nearby, on the other side, together with the brigade commanders. This was, I think, after he issued the order to continue the operation towards Potocari, and the brigade commanders resisted in a certain sense for the reasons I explained when answering questions by my Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as a result of the brigade commanders complaining, General Mladic actually held the troops up for at least a day and didn't send them off to Potocari; is that right? According to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 11th to the 12th, the order was that all units should stop at the lines they had reached. And after the meeting in Bratunac, all the units were pulled from those lines towards the town, and they were withdrawn to former positions in the direction of Viogora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That occurred after the brigade commanders complained to General Mladic that, "We shouldn't go further. We don't know where the 28th Division is"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was said that we had no contact with the 28th Division because civilians were in Potocari and because they were still moving towards Potocari. So there was a possibility that, together with the civilians, there were forces from the 28th Division, and if the attack were to be continued towards Potocari, the consequences would be considerable on both sides and especially for the civilians. And the euphoria around the entry into Srebrenica was stimulated, as I have already said, by whose behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in this situation, the brigade commanders were able to reason with General Mladic and their decisions were followed -- excuse me -- their advice was followed?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was something that the brigade commanders had to do as commanders, as professional soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mladic listened to them?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was very angry, and then he gave the order stop at the lines reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in this photograph, number 770, you appear to be communicating with General Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That was precisely in connection with what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is the period in the -- about what time did you go into Srebrenica, just to clear up that, that day on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Commander of the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade informed General Mladic that a part of his unit had entered Srebrenica, then General Mladic ordered General Zivanovic and myself to follow him towards Srebrenica. We went along the route Pribicevac, Zeleni Jadar, Bojna, Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What time did you get into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the afternoon. Two or three hours after the airstrikes perhaps. I don't remember now exactly what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you had already been sidelined by General Mladic in a position where you were -- had no more authority or work to do for the operation?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't relieved of my duty as Chief of Staff, neither myself nor General Zivanovic as Corps Commander, but the command over the brigade commanders was taken over by Mladic. He ordered, he commanded, he took charge, and we simply followed him into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand. I don't want to go back over that ground, but my question was: This is at that time period where you had been -- I think the term we ended up agreeing on was "sidelined."

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Excuse me. I do have one question, if I may. Following what you just said, I'm having difficulty seeing the difference between the situation as General Mladic ordered the capture of Srebrenica, a change in the earlier plans from just isolating and reducing it, to a capture in which, I believe you testified, that you thought it was not time, it was not ready, but nobody asked your advice and it would have been completely out of character with the army regulations if you had proffered and said, "I think that's wrong. I don't think you should go into Srebrenica now." But yet in this situation, when General Mladic has gone on TV and said, "March on to Bratunac, march on to Potocari," you and the other brigade commanders, thinking that was wrong, felt that you had the duty and followed through on it to dissuade him. What was the difference that you were not so bound or reticent that you felt at the time he announced you move ahead on the capture of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply, the brigade commanders -- at least, that was my assessment -- had to respond in this way and to persuade Mladic that that was not a good thing, that there were civilians in Potocari, and that there could be serious consequences for the civilian population and also for the forces that had entered Srebrenica, and also the possibility of the presence of 28th Division forces in Potocari among the civilians. Those were the main reasons. The brigade commanders felt it was their duty to respond in this way and to persuade General Mladic not to continue, because it would have been crazy to continue the operation towards Potocari. And that can also clearly be seen on the previous map, the exhibit, that the units from Srebrenica in fact returned to where they were ordered to go, the area of Viogora, from where they were to proceed to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go now to Exhibit 771.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, did you see Lieutenant Colonel Popovic as you came into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice Lieutenant Colonel Popovic in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention to this Exhibit 771. Who is the man standing over your left shoulder?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By physical appearance and the way this person is dressed, there were many soldiers like that. It seems to me to be Lieutenant Colonel Popovic. He never came to the forward command post on one single day, nor did he come with me to Srebrenica, nor did I see him coming with Mladic or Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this photo refresh your recollection about his presence, bring back any images of him being present, any conversations you might have had with him in Srebrenica, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all, not at all. I said for reasons of my health also, my memory is not such that I can remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Zivanovic was in Srebrenica, the Corps Commander; you were in Srebrenica, the Chief of Staff. We now see Lieutenant Colonel Popovic as the assistant commander for security. Were you aware of his duties and his assignments at this time period, at this time in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. I was not at all aware of them, nor was he in any way engaged, throughout the duration of the operation up until the entrance into Srebrenica. I don't know what his assignments were from the Corps Commander. He is his assistant, just like I was. Of course, not like me in the absence of the commander, when I was acting as the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you acting as deputy commander at this time?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was the Chief of Staff. The Corps Commander was there and he was in command, and the Corps Commander at that time was at the forward command post at Srebrenica when the forces, troops entered town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you were in Srebrenica, did you hear General Mladic make that comment about, "Now it's time to take revenge upon the Turks"?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear that, all of it, because I wasn't able to go as fast as him, and as General Zivanovic. They went faster. But I did hear some of the details, especially when he ordered the continuation of the operation. I heard that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The term "Turks" is a derogatory terms for Muslims, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never used that term. Everybody has his own way of expressing himself, so I don't wish to comment upon what General Mladic said. For me, they were Muslims and Bosniaks, as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you comment on General Mladic's use of the term "Turks" in that context?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't wish to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You wouldn't support the use of that term in that context?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it were up to me, no. I didn't use the term myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General Krstic, it was used officially. We have here one of your command of the Drina Corps -- one of your official letters saying, "We have checked information that the Turks are dissembling equipment," and it is signed by General Major Skocajic. So it is used officially.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you cannot use that officially, not at all. For us, they were Muslims, at that time; and later on, after the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina gained independence, they were Bosniaks. But that was signed by General Skocajic. I had nothing to do with that. That was probably written at the time when I was absent and when he replaced me, while I was undergoing treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: 18th March 1995.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. I wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The command -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, there's a worse term for Muslims that we've heard in this trial. What term is that?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Witnesses frequently -- well, not frequently, but I notice them use the term "balija," a term of some sort, "balija."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is a profoundly offensive term for a Muslim, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I never used it, and the Muslims did use terms for the Serbs, such as "Chetnik," and that is derogatory too, especially used in the way they did and how they understood the term "Chetnik," the concept "Chetnik."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me again, but the word "Turk," the name "Turk" was not derogatory, was it? "Balija" is, but "Turk," what did it mean Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. when you used the word "Turk"?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably because they were Muslims and that area was for a long time, as you well know, for 500 years, in fact, under Turkish rule, so probably that term remained and dates back to those days, the days of Turkish rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it means that they are not part of the country; they belong to Turkey?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. They belong to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When the commander officer communicates to the public or to his troops in a manner derogatory, racially derogatory, what kind of message does that send the young troops in the field, when the term "Turks" is used or the term "balija" is used? How would you expect the young men -- the 18-year-olds, the 19-year-olds, the 20-year-olds -- to react to that kind of term?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I consider that this question is an obvious example and runs along the lines of your suggestions and guidelines given after the break today, so that I should like to ask the Prosecutor to be more concrete in posing his questions and linked to the events and facts. All this seems to me to be a comment on his part and to enter into surmise and conjecture and reactions to a situation which is not concrete and not based on fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, please reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you comment on the effect you might expect General Mladic's statement to have on the troops?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have a bad effect in the sense that it would encourage something that was not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What would it encourage that was not good?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when that is said by the commander of an army, then it is clear what kind of effect this is going to have on the ordinary soldier, words used like that and expressions of that kind in a situation when the soldiers come into contact with members of either the 28th Division or possibly with the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In particular, what would happen? What could happen when this contact occurs under this sort of incitement?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be serious repercussions than the ones that could be expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Violence, for example?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me now to -- I've already said, actually. I've already told you when I spoke about the fact that the attack should not be continued how the commanders reacted to that, and I think that when I talked about that, I answered your question, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You answered earlier, and you said, "Then it is clear what kind of an effect this is going to have on the ordinary soldier, words used like that and expressions of that kind in a situation where the soldiers come into contact with members of either the 28th Division..." but you don't give us an example of what effect might happen.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have provided you with an answer to your question. Perhaps there would be uncontrolled behaviour on the part of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is Drinski magazine? General, is your leg bothering you?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll keep it up until the break. Thank you for your concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's Drinski magazine?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Drinski magazine is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you heard of the publication of the Drina Corps called the Drinski?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paper Srpska Vojska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Srpska Vojska, I believe, is one of the magazines for the army of the Republika Srpska, but I believe the Drinski magazine -- if you recall the testimony of Mr. Butler, there was an article in Drinski about the Branjevo Military Farm, and Mr. Butler testified that he believed this Drinski was a magazine published for the Drina Corps. You were Chief of Staff and Commander for the Drina Corps. Have you heard of this magazine?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Zvornik Brigade had a magazine of some kind. Whether it was called the Drinski magazine, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that there is a problem in the interpretation, perhaps. If we're thinking of the same magazine, the name of the magazine is just Drinski or Drinski Novine but not Drinski magazine. Perhaps I'm wrong, but as far as I can recall, that is what it is. So when it is interpreted into Serbian, it is -- it might be the Drinski magazine, but it was only called Drinski or Drinski Novine. So perhaps this has led to some misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. With that clarification, I should like to ask Mr. McCloskey to rephrase his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you heard of a magazine called Drinski, whether it be Zvornik Brigade or --

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was something of that kind, a publication of that kind of the Zvornik Brigade. I think that, later on, the Drina Corps and its information service did publish a paper of this kind, and I think it had the same title.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall an interview you gave to Drinski?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Possibly I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that we are in need of a break at this point. So let's take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One brief question before we get to Drinski. Did you hear any of the commanders or any officers talk to their troops about the comment General Mladic made taking revenge upon the Turks?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When were the officers aware that the comment was made?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did anyone hear him make it while he was in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear him make it while he was in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember being close to him at that point in time to be able to hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you may have heard it, but you don't remember, or what? I don't understand your response.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember hearing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Making reference to page 66 of the interview with Mr. Ruez, line 13: "Q: So he was keeping his comments for the television, comments like, 'It's time to take revenge on the Turks.' He kept that for the television. He didn't use these kinds of words in front of his staff? A: We were not with him all the time. That was his usual conduct. Following the takeover of Srebrenica, everyone could hear what he was saying in front of the cameras, and that was when he said that we should go out to Potocari and take revenge on the Turks."

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that here, yes, from the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear it in Srebrenica? The comment was everyone could hear it.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember whether I heard it in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now if we could go to Drinski, and I've got copies of the entire magazine, as well as -- but it's only in B/C/S, but I do have full translated copies of the article that I'm going to be referring to, and this is Exhibit 744. And if we could present the General with the original magazine, it would probably be easiest, and if you could go to the article which is marked with a yellow sticky. And I would request, Your Honour, that we are allowed to get the original magazine back and go with the photocopy. And if we could put the English page -- General, if you could take a moment to familiarise yourself with that, with this interview and this article. For the record, this is publication Drinski, date November 1995. The headline of the article is "The Youngest, but an Elite Corps Already." The author is Vuk Kovacevic, entitled "Interview with Major General Radislav Krstic, Commander of the Drina Corps of the Army of the Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what is the page to be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 2. And if we could get a close-up of the top four paragraphs. That's great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, while the General is reading the article, I would have a suggestion to make. I see that this is quite a lengthy text given to us by the Prosecution. In view of the complete content of this article, perhaps my learned friends could provide us with such articles and such lengthy documents a couple of days in advance so that the General could have time to familiarise himself with the contents before the questions are asked, and that would save us a great deal of time. That would be my suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are some other lengthy documents related to this article that we have, in fact, given to the Defence because they are more lengthy than a two- or three-page article. The issue that is brought up by this article is particularly sensitive, and it is the belief of the Prosecution that the -- it is appropriate and the best way to get at the truth to provide it in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no question that it is important. The question is that if we give General Krstic enough time to read the document, we'll be waiting here in the meantime, and I think there could be a practical suggestion. You have other matters to address. We could leave this question to be addressed after the long break that we will have in half an hour's time. In that way, at least we would have -- General Krstic and the Defence would have 10, 15 minutes to read this document. Do you agree with this practical suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. President, I agree. I understand the point, and we'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Visnjic, is this solution acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were not speaking into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's what we will do. Please go on to your next question, Mr. McCloskey, and after the break, you can go back to this area since the Defence and General Krstic at least will have had a little time to review the document, because we will see -- I said "review," because later on we will see what the position of General Krstic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Krstic, I think I asked you yesterday when you became reactivated after being sidelined, but now I want to ask you when General Zivanovic became reactivated after he was sidelined. On the afternoon of July 10th, you testified he was sidelined, put out of the command chain. Did he become reactivated at some point where he was allowed to have command authority again?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After which date? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said yesterday that on the afternoon of July 10th, General Mladic took over direct command and sidelined you and General Zivanovic. So I would like to know, after the afternoon of July 10th, when was it that General Zivanovic gained some sort of command authority again?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, when General Zivanovic started again to carry out assignments related to Srebrenica, but General Zivanovic was the Corps Commander, and he carried out his duties and responsibilities as envisaged by establishment for the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did he start to carry out his duties as Corps Commander?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very fact that General Zivanovic attended the meeting in the evening at the Command of the Bratunac Brigade, which was chaired by General Mladic, and before that he attended the meeting with representatives of the Dutch Battalion at the UNPROFOR, confirms what I said and my position that General Zivanovic was the Corps Commander. As to whether he carried out any assignments linked to Srebrenica and everything else that happened after the forces of the Drina Corps left to go towards Zepa, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you believe he regained his authority to command on the night of the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he discussed with General Zivanovic -- with General Mladic, I'm sorry. General Zivanovic was the Corps Commander and General Mladic the Commander-In-Chief of the VRS. I don't know what they discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were still, on July 11th, still the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, and General Zivanovic was still the Corps Commander. You've testified he had no power after July 11th. Can you clarify the issue of when he regained power?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. It is a very, very difficult question to ask me when my commander was reactivated. He was not relieved of duty. Whether he carried out any tasks after the 11th of July in connection with Srebrenica, whether that was done at his orders or following his instructions or those of General Mladic, that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you aware that he ever took command authority between the 11th and the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Zivanovic was at the command post. Whether he was in Vlasenica or somewhere else, I don't know that. He did issue some orders, and I spoke about those during the examination-in-chief, when I was

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, I'm sorry for interrupting you. General Krstic, when you met General Zivanovic at Srebrenica, did you speak amongst yourselves about the situation in the corps command?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I could not discuss such things with my superior officer. That would be an insult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can understand your answer, but let me put the question differently. Did your commander speak with you, the second in command, about the situation regarding the corps command?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Are you referring only to the situation around Srebrenica or in general?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you wish, you can begin by answering the question regarding the situation in general.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Zivanovic was the Corps Commander. The very fact that he came together with General Mladic speaks for itself. On the 9th, in the afternoon, he arrived at the forward command post in Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So General Zivanovic did not speak with you, but you observed that he agreed absolutely with General Mladic, he was in agreement with General Mladic; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a fact that he did not oppose General Mladic in any way when the question of the continuation of the attack was to be done, after his orders had been carried out, and also with regard to the entry into Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to make things quite clear, and it is not a play of words, you know that General Zivanovic did not oppose, but you don't know whether he was in agreement, whether he was in agreement; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm sorry, Mr. McCloskey, for interrupting. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE ATTORNEY
utterances.text: Between the period of July 11th and July 15th, was the Drina Corps command eliminated in any way in the area of Zvornik and Bratunac by the actions of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have also spoken about that. I spoke about it during the examination-in-chief, that is to say, when I was asked by the attorney. From the moment that General Mladic ordered a continuation of the attack, and then the entrance into the town itself, and then his position, the position taken at the meeting in the command of the Bratunac Brigade, in fact, his order -- not his position but his order -- at the suggestion and proposal of the commander of the Zvornik Brigade that it was not a good idea to go on to performing the next assignment because we had no contact at all with the forces of the 28th Division, and when he said, "That is not your concern. That is my concern. I am in command in this area," and this was followed by his order of the 17th of July, and the continued presence of him or his assistants, some of his assistants in that area, sufficiently illustrates the fact that General Mladic, with his assistants, had taken over command of the area of -- the Srebrenica area and the area of responsibility of Milic and Zvornik, and especially when it came to the question of prisoners of war and the engagement of the units in that region with respect to the carrying out of the assignment and the breakthrough of the 28th Division and, later on, the treatment of those prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE ATTORNEY
utterances.text: So General Zivanovic, under that theory, would have no authority to issue orders regarding prisoners or anything else?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Zivanovic, as far as I recall, wrote several orders by which he linked himself up with the orders of the Main Staff and so conveyed them on to the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have one question there. General Krstic, was it your impression that during this same period we're talking about, the 11th to the 15th or 16th, the 28th Division, along with the civilians in the column which was moving towards Tuzla was having some kind of engagements with the army along the way, and, in, fact, I think you testified there was some casualties, to your knowledge. Was it your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. impression that General Mladic and his people were also running the show, giving the orders about the activities of the soldiers who were engaged in actual capture and combat with the column of the 28th that was moving down or just with relation to the prisoners of war, as you have just testified? I just want to clarify that. Did you think that he'd taken over the entire operation, including any combat that might be between the column and the 28th and the soldiers in Zvornik or just the treatment of the POWs?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When speaking about the conflict between the civilians in the column and the members of the army, I don't think I can comment there, but I will answer your question in the following way: When it comes to the prisoners of war, I truly did gain the impression that General Mladic, he himself or his assistants, were in charge of all that. At the forward command post at Krivaca, 14th, an order of that kind arrived, and it was brought to my attention and sent on from the Corps Command to me. And in amongst other things, it spoke about the breakthrough of the 28th Division, the possible activities, their possible activities and operations, and the capture of members of the 28th Division. It also speaks, among other things, of where those POWs should be put up. So until that time and later on either, I had no knowledge about the prisoners of war. And the very fact that this order was sent to me from Krivaca towards Zepa was only sent -- I was only to be -- this was only to be brought to my attention, which meant that I had no responsibility and no involvement in the affair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just one follow-up. However, you have testified that -- I believe, that roughly 80 per cent of some of the divisions, Zvornik and Bratunac, were still down in their areas, even though their commanders were up with you with a smaller percentage, and we've seen many intercepts and orders dealing with some combat that was going on in the Zvornik area. My question was simply whether or not it was your impression at the time that Mladic was running the show as to how that combat would be carried on or whether that combat was still coming up to the regular brigade officers and the regular structure of the -- up to the point of capture, up to the point that anyone was captured, whether the actual fighting was still being run by the normal brigade structures.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about the forces that remained at the front, that they were engaged in the front towards Tuzla, Zivinice, and Kladanj, and Olovo, that is that 80 per cent of the overall forces of the brigades that were committed at the front. And the basic preoccupation of those troops was the defence, defence from these axes if there should be any activity, that is to say, involvement of the forces of the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if they were involved. And one of the tasks of the Zvornik and Bircani Brigade was also to take care and take steps to defend themselves from the forces of the 28th Division that attacked them from the rear, from the back. And I had some information when I came from Srebrenica to Vlasenica, to the command post of the corps, when I was involved about that by the officer on duty, who told me that the breakthrough of the 28th Division had taken place towards Tuzla and towards the Zvornik and Bircani Brigade. But everything that took place later on, the orders that I received, first and foremost on the 13th and then later on when it came to the involvement of the brigades towards Zepa, we could clearly see in the order regarding Zepa that these forces were engaged towards Zepa but that somebody was ordering mobilisation and assigning other tasks to them, and I truly did gain the impression at the time that it was the Main Staff that was in command there and the very fact that General Zivanovic himself was linking himself up in his order to the 13th and to the order from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to refer the General to some of the interview. This is the redacted version of the interview with Mr. Ruez. It's Exhibit 399A. And while you're looking for that, we can ask -- I can ask a couple of other questions.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE ATTORNEY
utterances.text: General, on the night of the 11th, you said you spent the night in the Bratunac Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't spend the night there but I slept in one of the rooms of the command of the Bratunac Brigade, Bratunac Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. For your search, that's 399A bis.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE ATTORNEY
utterances.text: What room did you sleep in?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I really don't remember which room I slept in. It is very difficult to say, to be able to say that now.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE ATTORNEY
utterances.text: Was Dalibor Krstic and Mr. Tosic with you at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I lay down, when I went to sleep, they were in front of the headquarters. The soldiers were not allowed to enter the headquarters. So when I went to bed, I don't actually know where they were put up, accommodated. Probably with the soldiers somewhere, with the soldiers of the Bratunac Brigade, on the premises where they were sleeping.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE ATTORNEY
utterances.text: Were arrangements made for you to stay at the Hotel Fontana on the 11th or any other time?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It is possible. It is possible. But as always, I slept where I was closer to my units; that is to say, I never availed myself of the comforts offered me at that time. But quite possibly some arrangements had been made. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to Exhibit -- have you found the interview? It's 399A bis.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE ATTORNEY
utterances.text: General, if you could look -- in the B/C/S version it should be page 11 and 12; in the English version it's page 19. And if you could put page 19 on the ELMO, and paragraph 3 is the paragraph I'm concerned about. And it's a long answer and covers various topics, but the answer that I wanted to try to get some clarification on was in paragraph -- what is paragraph 3 in the English. But it says: "The commander of the forces that were to go on to Zepa, I was designated to be the commander by the commander of the Main Staff, while for the area of Srebrenica and Bratunac, by the order of the commander of the Main Staff, remained the commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. May I just take a moment to read through the passage?

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE ATTORNEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that assertion here on page 11.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE ATTORNEY
utterances.text: Page 11 through 12. Sometimes it's hard to sort out the actual pages because they're so different. It begins, "The commander of the forces that were to go on to Zepa, I was designated to be the commander by the commander of the Main Staff."

utterances.speaker: RADISLAV KRSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. We can read through this.
